title: Meteorites in the Desert
summary: What meteors and meteorites are, why deserts like Saudi Arabia's Empty Quarter are good places to find them, and what these ancient rocks teach scientists.
poll: Looking for meteorites is a better hobby than collecting ordinary rocks.

versions.title: Rocks from Space
versions.text:
Have you seen a shooting star? It is not a star. It is a rock from space. In space, it is a meteoroid.

The rock zooms down. It gets so hot. It glows! The streak of light is a meteor. Most burn up. But some bits hit the ground. A rock that lands is a meteorite.

As it falls, it melts a bit. It gets a thin black crust.

Some are stone. Some are iron. Iron ones weigh a lot. A magnet sticks to them.

The desert is a good place to look. A dark rock stands out on tan sand. The air is dry. So the rocks last. Few plants hide them.

In 1932, a man went to the Empty Quarter. It is in Saudi Arabia. He found big pits in the sand. Each pit is a crater. An iron rock from space made them. In 1965, a huge chunk was found. Now it is in Riyadh.

These rocks are so old! They are older than the rocks of Earth. They help us learn how Earth was made.

Did you find a strange rock? Show it to a grown-up.

versions.title: Meteorites: Desert Treasures from Space
versions.text:
On a clear night in the desert, you may notice a bright streak flashing across the sky. People often call it a shooting star, although it is not a star at all; instead, it is a piece of rock or metal from space. While it is still drifting through space, astronomers call the object a meteoroid.

When a meteoroid plunges into Earth's atmosphere at tremendous speed, rubbing against the air heats it so much that it glows, producing a bright trail called a meteor. Most meteors are no larger than grains of sand, so they burn up completely, but occasionally a piece survives the fiery fall and reaches the ground, and that piece is called a meteorite.

During the fall, the meteorite's outer surface melts and then hardens again, forming a thin, glassy black coating known as a fusion crust, which is one of the clearest signs that a rock came from space.

Scientists usually divide meteorites into stony types and iron types, along with rare stony-iron mixtures. Iron meteorites are very dense, so they feel unexpectedly heavy for their size, and they usually attract a magnet.

Deserts are excellent places for finding meteorites, for several connected reasons. A dark, crusted rock contrasts sharply with pale sand, and because desert air is extremely dry, meteorites rust and wear away very slowly. Also, plants are scarce, so few of them hide the rocks, and researchers search Antarctica, which is actually a frozen desert, for the same reasons.

Saudi Arabia's Empty Quarter, the Rub al Khali, holds one of the most famous examples. In 1932, the explorer Harry St John Philby traveled to a remote spot there and recorded several craters, which are round holes dug out by an impact. Scientists later learned that an iron meteorite had broken apart and blasted out the Wabar craters, scattering metal pieces across the nearby dunes. In 1965, a gigantic iron chunk nicknamed the Camel's Hump, weighing about 2,200 kilograms, was recovered, and it is now displayed in Riyadh.

Meteorites are remarkably ancient. Most formed about 4.5 billion years ago, at the very beginning of our solar system, so they are much older than nearly any rock formed on Earth. By studying what they are made of, scientists gather valuable evidence about how the planets, including our own, first formed.

If you ever discover an unusual rock that might have fallen from the sky, show it to a teacher or another adult, because special laboratories can examine it and confirm whether it is truly a visitor from space.

wrong.C: The article does not warn against deserts.
wrong.D: The article does not compare explorers and scientists.

MID.prompt: Explain three reasons why deserts are good places to find meteorites. Use details from the article.
checklist: I gave three reasons from the article.
I explained why each reason helps people find meteorites.
I used at least one key word correctly.

keyWords.definition: the layer of gases surrounding a planet
keyWords.example: Mars has a much thinner atmosphere than Earth.

keyWords.definition: a bowl-shaped hole formed by an impact or explosion
keyWords.example: Scientists measured the crater to estimate the size of the object that made it.

keyWords.definition: having a lot of mass packed into a small space
keyWords.example: Gold is so dense that a small bar is surprisingly heavy.

keyWords.definition: to look very different from something next to it
keyWords.example: The white buildings contrast with the dark mountains behind them.
Archaeologists studied ancient tools found near the oasis.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Meteorites are ancient space rocks that deserts preserve and reveal.
Most meteors are dangerous to people who travel across deserts.
The Camel's Hump is the largest meteorite that has ever been found.
Antarctica is the only place on Earth where meteorites can be found.
questions.why: The article explains what meteorites are, why deserts preserve and reveal them, and what they teach.

wrong.B: The article says most meteors burn up completely.
wrong.C: The article does not say it is the largest ever found.
wrong.D: The article describes deserts such as the Empty Quarter, too.

questions.stem: What is a fusion crust, according to the article?
options: A layer of sand that blows over a crater after an impact
A glassy black coating made when the surface melts
The rocky outer layer of planet Earth beneath the soil
A crack that forms when a meteorite hits hard ground
questions.why: The article says the exterior melts and hardens again, forming a thin, glassy black coating called a fusion crust.

wrong.A: Sand in a crater is not a fusion crust.
wrong.C: Earth's crust is a different idea.
wrong.D: The article does not describe a crack.

questions.stem: Who recorded the Wabar craters in 1932?
options: A team of astronauts
The scientists who found the Camel's Hump
Harry St John Philby
Researchers from Antarctica
questions.why: The article states that the explorer Harry St John Philby recorded the craters in 1932.

wrong.B: The Camel's Hump was recovered in 1965, later than 1932.
wrong.D: Antarctica is mentioned for a different reason.

questions.stem: The article says a dark meteorite contrasts with pale sand. What does contrast mean in this sentence?
options: To melt into
To be hidden by
To weigh more than
To look very different from
questions.why: A dark rock on pale sand looks very different from its surroundings, which makes it easy to notice.

wrong.A: The rock does not melt into the sand.
wrong.B: Contrast makes the rock easier to see, not hidden.
wrong.C: Contrast here is about how things look, not weight.

questions.stem: Why do iron meteorites feel unexpectedly heavy for their size?
options: They are extremely dense.
They are full of sand.
They are covered with ice.
They are still hot from falling.
questions.why: The article says iron meteorites are extraordinarily dense, so they feel heavy for their size.

wrong.B: The article does not say meteorites contain sand.
wrong.C: Ice is not mentioned as a cause.
wrong.D: Heat does not make an object heavier.

questions.stem: Why would a meteorite be harder to find in a wet, green forest than in the Empty Quarter?
options: Forests have no rocks at all, so nothing can be found.
Plants could hide it, and moisture would rust it.
Meteorites cannot fall through the branches of tall trees.
Forest soil is magnetic and pulls meteorites underground.
questions.why: The article explains that deserts help because they are dry and have few plants, so the opposite conditions would make finding meteorites harder.

wrong.A: Forests have rocks; this is not the reason.
wrong.D: The article does not mention magnetic soil.

questions.stem: Why are meteorites valuable evidence about the early solar system?
options: They glow brightly as meteors before they reach the ground.
They are found only in Saudi Arabia and nowhere else.
Most are older than nearly any rock on Earth.
They are light and easy for scientists to lift and carry.
questions.why: Because most meteorites formed at the beginning of the solar system, their chemistry preserves clues about how the planets formed.

wrong.A: Glowing does not explain their scientific value.
wrong.B: The article mentions deserts worldwide and Antarctica.

questions.stem: How does the article organize its information about the space rock's names?
options: By comparing meteorites with volcanoes
By listing the names in alphabetical order
By describing only the final landing
By following the rock in sequence from space, through the atmosphere, to the ground
questions.why: The article follows the object as a meteoroid in space, a meteor in the atmosphere, and a meteorite on the ground.

wrong.B: The order follows the rock's journey, not the alphabet.
wrong.C: The article describes every stage of the journey.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say meteorites are just interesting rocks with no real value. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
